pos: n. (Berthold Haller, 1492–1536, preacher at the Bern Minster and reformer of Bern)
etymology: German Berthold, bright ruler, from Germanic beraht and wald; Haller, of Hall, a salt-works.
biblical_def: Berthold Haller was a Swabian who came to Bern as a schoolmaster in 1513, was made a canon and then preacher at the Minster, and found himself the leader of the Reformation in the most powerful canton of the Confederacy. He was by temperament the least likely man for it. His letters to Zwingli are a long record of fear: he asks repeatedly to be released, says he is not equal to the work, reports that his knees fail him before the council, and is told each time to stay where he is. He stayed thirteen years. He carried the city through the Bern Disputation of January 1528, where the Ten Theses were debated for nineteen days and the council then abolished the mass and the images; he drafted the Bern synodal order with Capito; and he held the new church together until his death in 1536. The dictionary records the fear as carefully as the outcome, because the two together are the lesson. “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness” (2Co 12:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines infirmity as an unsound state of the body, a failing or weakness, and a disputation as a controversy in words.
webster_full: INFIRM'ITY, n. An unsound or unhealthy state of the body; weakness; failing; foible.
DISPUTA'TION, n. A reasoning or argumentation in opposition; a controversy in words.
MIN'STER, n. A monastery; a cathedral church.
SUFFI'CIENT, a. Enough; equal to the end proposed; adequate to wants.
scriptures: And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness.
Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.
For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.
corruption_summary: The timid preacher who carried Bern through nineteen days of disputation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the heroic register of most Reformation writing, which prefers its reformers fearless and so either omits Haller or recasts his letters as modesty. They are not modesty; they are a frightened man asking to be let go, and the Reformation in Bern was carried by him anyway.

The principle to recover is that God's power is not supplied where weakness is absent but exactly where it is confessed: “for my strength is made perfect in weakness” (2Co 12:9). The promise Haller needed was not a change of temperament but a hand to hold him up, and that is what Isaiah offers: “I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness” (Isa 41:10).

pos: n. (Oswald Myconius, 1488–1552, schoolmaster, chief pastor of Basel and first biographer of Zwingli)
etymology: German Oswald, divine power, from Germanic os and wald; Myconius, a grecised form of his family name Geisshusler.
biblical_def: Oswald Myconius spent most of his life as a schoolmaster, which is the key to him. He taught at Basel, Zurich and Lucerne; it was he who brought Zwingli to the Great Minster at Zurich in 1518, and he who wrote the first life of Zwingli after Kappel. Driven from Lucerne for his evangelical teaching, he returned to Zurich as a schoolmaster, and in 1531, when Oecolampadius died, Basel called him to be its chief pastor and professor of New Testament though he had no doctorate and had never held a parish. He held the office for twenty-one years. He drafted the First Confession of Basel in 1534, defended the Reformed doctrine of the Supper against both the Lutheran and the bare-memorial accounts, and kept the university and the church in step. He is the dictionary's instance of a teacher's ministry: the men he taught and the friend he introduced to a pulpit did more than his own writings. “a whole year they assembled themselves with the church, and taught much people” (Act 11:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a schoolmaster as one who presides over and teaches a school, and to sharpen as to make keen or acute.
webster_full: SCHOOLMASTER, n. The man who presides over and teaches a school; a teacher; a preceptor.
SHARP'EN, v. To make sharp or keen; to make more eager, active or acute.
AN'TISTES, n. A chief priest or presiding minister; in the Swiss churches, the chief pastor of a city.
INTRODUCE', v. To lead or bring in; to bring into notice or acquaintance.
scriptures: And when he had found him, he brought him unto Antioch. And it came to pass, that a whole year they assembled themselves with the church, and taught much people. And the disciples were called Christians first in Antioch.
Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
And we beseech you, brethren, to know them which labour among you, and are over you in the Lord, and admonish you;
Phm 1:7
For we have great joy and consolation in thy love, because the bowels of the saints are refreshed by thee, brother.
corruption_summary: The schoolmaster who gave Zurich Zwingli and Basel twenty-one years of oversight.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the one the Reformation era itself nearly made: Basel hesitated to appoint a man with no degree, and modern accounts still measure Myconius against Oecolampadius and find him thin. He was not a first-rank theologian. He was the man who kept a university city's church sound for two decades and taught the generation that followed.

The principle to recover is that teaching and friendship are means of grace to the church and not preliminaries to the real work. Solomon's figure is of two men wearing each other to an edge: “Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend” (Pro 27:17). Paul asks the Thessalonians for the regard that such labour earns and does not announce itself: “to know them which labour among you, and are over you in the Lord” (1Th 5:12).

pos: n. (Simon Sulzer, 1508–1585, antistes of Basel, who drew the city toward the Lutheran doctrine of the Supper)
etymology: Hebrew Shimon, hearing, through Greek Simon; Sulzer, of Sulz, a brine-spring.
biblical_def: Simon Sulzer was a Bernese of ability who studied at Strasbourg and Wittenberg, taught at Bern, and from 1552 was professor and then antistes of Basel, which he governed for more than thirty years. He is in the dictionary as an honest negative. Sulzer came home from Germany persuaded that the difference between the Reformed and the Lutherans on the Lord's Supper was a quarrel about words, and he spent his career acting on it: he worked to bring Basel to subscribe the Augsburg Confession, admitted Lutheran preachers, and kept Basel from joining the other Swiss churches in subscribing the Second Helvetic Confession of 1566. Bern deposed him from his earlier post there for the same reason. The result was that Basel stood half out of the Swiss Reformed communion for a generation, and only after his death did it come fully back. A man may pursue unity by the one method that guarantees division, which is to treat a real difference as a verbal one. “The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ?” (1Co 10:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines communion as fellowship or a partaking of the Lord's Supper, and doctrine as whatever is taught as principle or position.
webster_full: COMMU'NION, n. Fellowship; intercourse; concord; the celebration of the Lord's Supper.
DOC'TRINE, n. Whatever is taught; principle or position in any science; the truths of the gospel.
SUBSCRI'BE, v. To assent to; to attest by writing one's name beneath.
COMPROMISE', n. A mutual promise or contract of two parties to abide by the decision of an arbitrator.
scriptures: The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?
Eph 4:14
That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive;
Gal 1:10
For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ.
Therefore, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle.
corruption_summary: The antistes who held Basel back from the Second Helvetic Confession.
corruption_paragraphs: Sulzer is the patron saint of a position that is perennially attractive: that confessional differences between Protestants are verbal, that the sacramental controversies were a tragedy of temperaments, and that a broad subscription is kinder than an exact one. It is worth saying what his method produced. Basel, the most learned city of the Swiss Reformation, was left for thirty years neither Reformed nor Lutheran, trusted by neither, and had to be recovered after his death. Vagueness bought nothing.

The principle to recover is that the Supper is a real communion with Christ's body and blood, received by faith, and that the question of how is therefore not a verbal one: “The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?” (1Co 10:16). Paul's warning about doctrinal instability names the exact mechanism — “tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine” (Eph 4:14) — and his remedy is to hold what was taught: “stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught” (2Th 2:15).

pos: n. (Kaspar Megander, 1495–1545, Zwinglian preacher at Bern, driven out over his catechism)
etymology: German Kaspar, from Persian through Latin Gaspar, treasurer; Megander, a grecised form of his family name Grossmann, great man.
biblical_def: Kaspar Megander was a Zurich man, a hospital chaplain and then a professor, who stood at Zwingli's side at the disputations and came to Bern in 1528 as its chief theologian after the Reformation was carried there. He wrote commentaries, taught in the Bern school, and in 1536 produced the Bern catechism, which stated the Lord's Supper in a plainly Zwinglian way. The following year Martin Bucer, pursuing concord with the Lutherans, came to Bern and persuaded the magistrates to let him revise the catechism toward a stronger account of Christ's presence. Megander refused the altered text as a corruption of what he had written, and the council dismissed him; he went back to Zurich and died there in 1545. Bucer meant well and acted badly: he had a city's catechism rewritten over its author's head by a foreign negotiator. “To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you” (Gal 2:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a catechism as a form of instruction by questions and answers, and a trust as something committed to one's care.
webster_full: CAT'ECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
TRUST, n. Something committed to a person's care for use or management.
REVI'SE, v. To review; to re-examine; to look over with care for correction.
CON'CORD, n. Agreement between persons; union in opinion or sentiment.
scriptures: Gal 2:5
To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you.
O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called:
That good thing which was committed unto thee keep by the Holy Ghost which dwelleth in us.
Rev 3:11
Behold, I come quickly: hold that fast which thou hast, that no man take thy crown.
corruption_summary: The catechist of Bern, dismissed when a foreign mediator rewrote his book.
corruption_paragraphs: The Megander affair is usually filed under the history of Protestant concord, with Bucer the far-sighted peacemaker and Megander the rigid Zwinglian who could not see past a formula. The dictionary does not accept the framing. Whatever the merits of Bucer's doctrine of the Supper — and the Reformed churches eventually went a good way toward it — the method was wrong: a confessional document was altered by an outside negotiator with the magistrates' backing and against its author's judgment, and the author lost his place for saying so.

The principle to recover is that a trust committed to a minister is to be kept rather than traded, and that the pressure to give way is strongest when it comes dressed as peace: “That good thing which was committed unto thee keep by the Holy Ghost which dwelleth in us” (2Ti 1:14). Paul's refusal at Jerusalem was a refusal of an hour's concession in a cause that looked small: “no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you” (Gal 2:5).

pos: n. (Sebastian Hofmeister, 1476–1533, Franciscan doctor and reformer of Schaffhausen)
etymology: Latin Sebastianus, of Sebaste, venerable; Hofmeister, steward of a household; grecised by him as Oeconomus.
biblical_def: Sebastian Hofmeister was a Franciscan who took his doctorate at Paris and was a lector of his order at Constance and Zurich before the gospel took hold of him. He was one of the ablest debaters on the evangelical side at the second Zurich disputation of 1523, where he argued the case against images and the mass, and he was afterwards sent to his native Schaffhausen to reform it. He carried a good part of the town and then lost it: the council turned against him under pressure from the Catholic cantons, and he was expelled in 1525. He spent the rest of his short life preaching at Zurich, at Bern — where he was among the leading disputants in the great debate of 1528 — and at Zofingen, where he died in 1533. He is the dictionary's case of a reformer whose gifts were for the public contest rather than the settled charge, and who was used accordingly, moved from town to town wherever the argument had to be made. “And he spake boldly in the name of the Lord Jesus, and disputed against the Grecians” (Act 9:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a gainsayer as one who opposes or contradicts, and defence as vindication, justification, apology.
webster_full: GAINSA'YER, n. One who opposes or contradicts; an opposer.
DEFENCE', n. Vindication; justification; apology; a plea or answer.
LEC'TOR, n. A reader; in religious orders, one appointed to read and lecture.
CONVINCE', v. To persuade or satisfy the mind by evidence; to convict.
scriptures: Act 9:29
And he spake boldly in the name of the Lord Jesus, and disputed against the Grecians: but they went about to slay him.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Php 1:17
But the other of love, knowing that I am set for the defence of the gospel.
Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ;
corruption_summary: The Franciscan doctor who argued the Reformation from town to town.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a general distaste for the whole genre of the public disputation, which is now read as theatre: a staged debate whose outcome the council had decided beforehand. The Zurich and Bern records do not support it. The sessions ran for days on the text of Scripture, both sides spoke, and in Hofmeister's own Schaffhausen the vote eventually went the other way, which a rigged contest does not do.

The principle to recover is that an elder must be able to answer opposition and not merely to assert, which is a required qualification and not a gift some have: “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9). Paul describes the work in military figures because it is work: “Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God” (2Co 10:5).

pos: n. (Joachim Vadian, 1484–1551, humanist, physician and mayor of St Gallen, who reformed the city as a layman)
etymology: Hebrew Yehoyaqim, the LORD raises up, through Joachim; Vadian, a latinised form of von Watt.
biblical_def: Joachim Vadian is the Reformation's clearest instance of a magistrate who was also its theologian. Born at St Gallen, he went to Vienna, became professor of poetry, rector of the university in 1516, and a physician and geographer of European reputation; then he came home, married, was made town physician and in 1526 mayor of St Gallen, and held that office for most of the next twenty-five years. He had come to the evangelical faith through Scripture and through Zwingli, who was his friend and in whose circle he stood; and from the mayor's chair he carried the abolition of the mass in 1527, dissolved the great abbey's hold on the town where he could, corresponded with every Reformed theologian of the day, and wrote on the Supper against both Rome and the Anabaptists. He was never ordained and never claimed to be. A layman in civil office, studying the Scriptures and governing a city by them, is a pattern the dictionary holds up deliberately. “for he was a faithful man, and feared God above many” (Neh 7:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a burgomaster as the chief magistrate of a city, and a layman as one not a clergyman.
webster_full: BUR'GOMASTER, n. A burgh-master; the chief magistrate of a city or town.
LA'YMAN, n. One of the people, as distinct from the clergy; a man not in orders.
PHYSI'CIAN, n. A person skilled in the art of healing; one whose profession is to prescribe remedies.
MAG'ISTRATE, n. A public civil officer invested with the executive government, or some branch of it.
scriptures: Neh 7:2
That I gave my brother Hanani, and Hananiah the ruler of the palace, charge over Jerusalem: for he was a faithful man, and feared God above many.
Pro 29:4
The king by judgment establisheth the land: but he that receiveth gifts overthroweth it.
Rom 13:3
For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil. Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power? do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the same:
For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty.
corruption_summary: The mayor of St Gallen, a layman who reformed his own city.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse cuts two ways in our own day. Some use a figure like Vadian to argue that ordination is a formality and that any learned Christian may do a minister's work; others use the same figure to argue that Christian magistrates should govern as churchmen. Vadian did neither. He never preached in the church and never pretended to the office, and he governed as a magistrate while submitting to the ministry of the word like any other member.

The principle to recover is that the two offices are distinct and both are God's, and that a believing magistrate's duty is to govern justly rather than to pastor: “For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil” (Rom 13:3). Paul tells the church what to ask for such men, and the end asked for is the quiet in which the gospel can be preached: “that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty” (1Ti 2:2).

pos: n. (Johannes Kessler, 1502–1574, saddler, reader and preacher at St Gallen, chronicler of the Reformation)
etymology: Latin Johannes, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Kessler, a coppersmith, a maker of kettles.
biblical_def: Johannes Kessler was a St Gallen boy sent to study at Wittenberg, and on the road in March 1522 he and a companion fell in at the Black Bear inn at Jena with a knight in a red cap reading a Hebrew psalter, who paid for their supper and questioned them about Wittenberg; it was Luther coming down from the Wartburg, and Kessler's account of the evening is the best-known eyewitness page in Reformation literature. He came home to a city that could not pay him as a preacher, so he learned the saddler's trade and worked at it for twenty years while teaching the Scriptures in the artisans' reading-schools of St Gallen, where craftsmen met to have the Bible read and expounded. He wrote the Sabbata, a chronicle of the Swiss Reformation as he saw it. Only in 1542 was he given a regular charge, and in 1571 he became the city's chief pastor. A tradesman who taught the Bible at a workbench for two decades. “And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought” (Act 18:3).

webster_full: SAD'DLER, n. One whose occupation is to make saddles.

corruption_summary: The saddler who taught Scripture at a workbench and met Luther at an inn.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern use made of the St Gallen reading-schools by those who argue from them that the church needs no ordained ministry, since artisans read and expounded the Bible among themselves. Kessler himself sought and eventually accepted a regular call, and the reading-schools operated under the city's ministers, not instead of them.

The principle to recover is that a man who must earn his bread with his hands is not thereby disqualified from teaching, and that the apostles set the precedent on purpose: “Yea, ye yourselves know, that these hands have ministered unto my necessities” (Act 20:34). Paul tells the Thessalonians why he did it: “labouring night and day, because we would not be chargeable unto any of you, we preached unto you the gospel of God” (1Th 2:9).

pos: n. (Johann Haller, 1523–1575, dean and chief pastor of Bern, who returned the city to the Reformed confession)
etymology: German Johann, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Haller, of Hall, a salt-works.
biblical_def: Johann Haller — no relation to Berthold, and a generation later — was a Bernese who studied at Zurich under Bullinger, served at Augsburg until the Interim drove the Reformed out, and came home in 1548 to be dean and then chief pastor of Bern, which he remained for twenty-seven years. His task was repair. Bern had been pulled toward the Lutheran account of the Supper by the men around Simon Sulzer, its own catechism had been altered over its author's head, and it was no longer clear what the canton confessed. Haller worked patiently with Bullinger's counsel to settle the question, had the Lutheranising party removed, and in 1566 brought Bern to subscribe the Second Helvetic Confession, which fixed the canton in the Reformed communion for good. He was not an original theologian and did not need to be. “ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls” (Jer 6:16).

corruption_summary: The dean who brought Bern back and signed the Second Helvetic Confession.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the preference, in church writing and church practice alike, for the founder over the restorer. Berthold Haller has a monument in Bern and Johann Haller is barely known, though the settled Reformed character of that canton is more his work than anyone's. Repair is slow, unglamorous and mostly invisible when it succeeds.

The principle to recover is that recovering an old position is a legitimate and often necessary labour, and Scripture commends it in just those terms: “Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16). Hebrews names the drift Haller had to reverse and the ground of stability: “Be not carried about with divers and strange doctrines. For it is a good thing that the heart be established with grace” (Heb 13:9).

pos: n. (Benedikt Aretius, c. 1505–1574, Bernese professor of theology, commentator and botanist)
etymology: Latin Benedictus, blessed; Aretius, a grecised form of his family name Marti, from Greek arete, virtue.
biblical_def: Benedikt Aretius, born Benedikt Marti near Bern, taught Greek and Hebrew and then theology in the Bern academy for most of his life. He wrote commentaries on the whole New Testament that were reprinted for a century and a compact system of divinity, and he was at the same time one of the first serious botanists of the Alps, climbing after plants and publishing a catalogue of them — a combination the dictionary notes with approval, since the book of nature and the book of Scripture were not rivals to him. His sharpest work was doctrinal. When the Italian anti-Trinitarian Valentinus Gentilis was tried at Bern in 1566 and executed, Aretius published the proceedings with a full defence of the doctrine of the Trinity from Scripture, and that treatise is why he is remembered. The dictionary affirms the doctrine without endorsing the penalty: the Confederacy's sword was not the instrument Christ appointed against heresy. “For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one” (1Jo 5:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the Trinity as the union of three persons in one Godhead, and a commentary as a series of comments or annotations.
webster_full: TRIN'ITY, n. The union of three persons in one Godhead, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.
COM'MENTARY, n. A comment; exposition; explanation; a book of annotations on a text.
BOT'ANY, n. That branch of natural history which treats of vegetables.
HER'ESY, n. A fundamental error in religion; an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine.
scriptures: For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one.
Joh 1:1
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
Joh 17:3
And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.
corruption_summary: The Bern commentator who defended the Trinity and catalogued Alpine plants.
corruption_paragraphs: The anti-Trinitarian case that Aretius answered is not a sixteenth-century curiosity; it is revived in every generation, and its modern form argues that the Trinity is a Greek philosophical imposition on a Hebrew book. The answer Aretius gave is still the answer: the doctrine is not deduced from metaphysics but gathered from the text, from the Word who was with God and was God, from the one name into which the nations are baptised, and from the three that bear record.

The principle to recover is that orthodoxy is defended from Scripture and not by the magistrate's sword, and here the dictionary parts from Bern in 1566 while holding the doctrine Bern was defending. The baptismal formula is the plainest witness and belongs to the church, not the council: “baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost” (Mat 28:19). And eternal life is set in the knowledge of the Father and the Son together: “that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent” (Joh 17:3).

pos: n. pl. (the ten articles debated at the Bern Disputation of January 1528, by which Bern was reformed)
etymology: thesis, from Greek thesis, a setting down, a proposition laid down for debate; Bern, the chief city of the Swiss Confederacy.
biblical_def: The Ten Theses of Bern were the propositions on which the Bernese council staged a public disputation from 6 to 26 January 1528, with Zwingli, Oecolampadius, Bucer, Capito and Hofmeister on the evangelical side and the bishops invited but mostly absent. They were drafted by Berthold Haller and Franz Kolb with Zwingli's help, and they move in order: the holy Christian church, whose only head is Christ, is born of the word of God and abides in it and hears no stranger's voice; it makes no laws apart from that word; the ceremonies it has added obscure Christ; Christ's one sacrifice is perfect and the mass therefore contradicts the gospel; Christ is not bodily in the bread and wine; the invocation of saints and the images set up in churches are without warrant; the compulsory celibacy of the clergy is a cause of unchastity. After nineteen days the council abolished the mass, removed the images, and reformed the canton. It is the most thorough of the Swiss disputations and the briefest Reformed confession of its decade. “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me” (Joh 10:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a thesis as a position or proposition laid down and maintained by argument, and head as a chief, a principal person.
webster_full: THE'SIS, n. A position or proposition which a person advances and offers to maintain by argument.
HEAD, n. A chief; a principal person; a leader; a commander; one who has the first rank.
AR'TICLE, n. A single clause or item; a distinct proposition in a creed or confession.
CER'EMONY, n. Outward rite; external form in religion; forms of civility.
scriptures: My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me:

For the husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the church: and he is the saviour of the body.
Col 1:18
And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence.
Eph 2:20
And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone;
corruption_summary: Nineteen days of debate in January 1528, and ten articles that reformed a canton.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard modern account of the Swiss disputations makes them political instruments: the magistrates decided first and arranged a debate to legitimate the decision. The Bern record resists it. The city had twice refused to move, the Catholic cantons pressed it hard, the council invited the bishops and gave their representatives the floor, and the proceedings were printed in full so that the argument could be weighed by anyone. A council that wanted a rubber stamp would not have sat nineteen days over Scripture.

The principle to recover is the first thesis itself, which is the whole Reformation in one clause: that the church is born of the word of God, abides in it, and does not hear the voice of a stranger. That is the Lord's own description of his flock — “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me” (Joh 10:27) — and the headship which the theses put beyond dispute is Paul's: “And he is the head of the body, the church” (Col 1:18).
